implementation_notes: java.util.concurrent supplies the whole structure: extend RecursiveTask<V> (or RecursiveAction for void work), split in compute() into two subtasks, fork one and compute the other on the current thread, then join; ForkJoinPool.submit/invoke executes the root and its workers steal from each other's deques, which is what makes recursive decomposition pay off. The framework's own guideline is the cut-off: if the task is small enough, solve it directly with a loop. Parallel streams (Arrays.parallelSort, collection.parallelStream) are the same pool behind a data-parallel API and replace the hand-written recursion whenever the work is expressible as stream operations.
pitfalls: Fork both halves and the current thread has nothing to do before the join; fork one side and compute the other.
The pool is sized for CPU-bound work: blocking on I/O or a lock inside compute() starves the workers and can stall the whole pool.
A mutable accumulator shared by forked tasks is a data race; combine the join() results instead.

variants.name: CompletableFuture fan-out
variants.implementation_notes: The fork/combine pair becomes supplyAsync(fn, pool) returning a CompletableFuture plus thenCombine (two branches) or allOf (n branches) for the join, so the recursion is written as a tree of future combinators instead of RecursiveTask.compute() calls - the executor stays an explicit choice rather than the framework's pool. Choose this lane when the branches have different result types, when the caller must stay non-blocking, or when the decomposition must be composed with other asynchronous work; the classic RecursiveTask still wins when the split/join itself must be tuned, because recursive fork/join through work-stealing deques is exactly what ForkJoinPool optimises.
pitfalls: thenCombine runs the combiner on whichever thread completes last: a blocking combiner parks a pool thread.
Without an explicit executor the async stages run on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), competing with every parallel stream in the process.
Exceptions are captured in the future and only surface at join/get: a missing exceptionally/handle leaves failures invisible.

variants.name: Virtual threads per task
variants.implementation_notes: Java 21's Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() starts one virtual thread per submitted task, so each split can be submitted and joined with Future.get without managing a bounded platform-thread pool. Virtual threads exist so that tasks which block (I/O, remote calls, locks) scale to very high numbers - they do not make CPU-bound recursion faster - so this lane is for decompositions whose leaves block, while the ForkJoinPool work-stealing lane stays the default for arithmetic. Note the runtime's pinning rule: inside synchronized blocks or native frames a virtual thread cannot unmount, so a blocking leaf held there consumes its carrier.
pitfalls: Virtual threads do not accelerate CPU-bound recursion; use them for blocking leaves, not to replace the fork/join pool.
Pinning inside synchronized blocks or native frames can exhaust the carrier threads while looking like a hang.
Per-task creation is cheap but not free: spawning a virtual thread per leaf below the cut-off still costs more than the leaf work.
